There was a version of that decision that was humble, maybe, education as building, course by course, and a version that was just a habit handed down for centuries until nobody remembered to ask. He suspected both were true at once, and he liked that suspicion more than he could explain.

Mr. Wilson was at the folding table near the garage, cutting lime wedges with the concentration of a man performing surgery. He had coached Liam in track for four years and had a habit of granting amnesty for small crimes, missed practices, once a thrown baton, provided you ran the hills on Saturday. When Liam and Patrick drifted over, still arguing about whether the cap was a compliment or an insult, Mr. Wilson listened with his head tilted, knife paused.

"You two are asking that question at a party," he said. "In August you'll be asking questions in a lecture hall. It's the same thing, you know. Nobody makes you do it. That's the whole trick."

The music changed to something with a bass line you could feel in the teeth, and Shayden's little brother began conducting it from the porch railing with somebody's stolen cap. Down the street, a girl from Liam's calculus class was trying to parametrize the wind, arms out, turning her body like a compass needle to map where each gust came from, and her friends were laughing, and she was laughing too, but she kept turning. Liam thought about telling her what he'd figured out about the cap, about bricklayers, about how everything he'd learned in four years seemed to be either a tool that had forgotten its purpose or a purpose still searching for its tool. He couldn't decide which the mortarboard was. Maybe he'd find out in college. Maybe he'd find out the answer was both, again, always both.

The wind came back, a long slow tectonic shove of it that moved the whole canopy over the food table six inches on its legs, and Liam's cap lifted and went tumbling across the lawn, end over end, square and ridiculous and somehow still flying. Patrick shouted something. Liam was already running, gown flapping behind him like a flag, punch spilling cold and sticky over his wrist, and the cap rolled to a stop against the fence, tilted up on one corner as if it were trying to listen.

He picked it up and put it on backwards.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes a typical payday loan fee of $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks equals an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent.
story:
The dealership's showroom smelled like new carpet and coffee that had sat too long, and John stood between a silver hatchback and a red coupe while his mother signed papers at a desk across the room. She had told him to wait, so he waited, drifting along the row of cars with their window stickers angled like little white sails. Flavie was beside him because she'd needed a ride after her shift and nowhere else to be, and Mathys had tagged along because Mathys always tagged along.

"It's three hundred short," Flavie said. She said it quietly, to the sticker on the coupe, which read 5.9% APR for sixty months. "Rent's due Friday, and my mom can't cover it till her next check, which is three weeks out."

John had been reading the sticker without really seeing it. Now he saw it twice, once as numbers and once as Flavie's voice. "What's the APR on that?" he asked, pointing.

Mathys leaned in, squinting. "Annual percentage rate. It's on everything." He had a habit of beginning sentences as though no one else had ever read anything. Their economics teacher, Ms. Toussaint, called it pontificating, and had once made him look the word up in front of the class, which had quieted him for almost a week.

"I know what APR is," Flavie said. "What I don't have is three hundred dollars."

"There's a place on Delmore," Mathys said. "FastCash or whatever. You just walk in with a pay stub. Fifteen bucks per hundred, two weeks, then you pay it back. Forty-five dollars to borrow three hundred. That's nothing."

John's mother was still at the desk, leaning over a payment schedule while the salesman slid a pen toward her. John watched her write her signature and thought about the sticker again, the 5.9% stretched over five years, and how she'd said last night that the car would end up costing more than the price on the window. He'd asked why, and she'd said, "Interest. Borrowed money costs more over time. That's how it works both ways, too; my savings account pays me a little for keeping money in it." She hadn't gone further, and he hadn't asked.

Flavie had gone quiet. She was doing something with her mouth that meant she was calculating.

"Wait," John said. "Say the fee again."

"Fifteen per hundred, for two weeks," Mathys said. "It's posted right on the window. My cousin used them twice."

John took out his phone and opened the browser. Flavie watched him type, her arms folded. He found a page from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and read it, then read it again, because the first time he thought he'd misread.

"It says here a typical payday loan fee of fifteen dollars per hundred borrowed, for two weeks, works out to an annual percentage rate of almost four hundred percent."

Mathys laughed, one short syllable. "That can't be right. Forty-five bucks on three hundred is nothing."

"That's for two weeks," John said. "A year is twenty-six of those. The rate isn't the fee, it's the fee stretched over a year. That's what APR is for." He turned the screen toward Flavie, who took the phone and read it herself, her thumb hovering.

"Almost four hundred percent," she said.

Ms. Toussaint had made them do a savings problem just last month: two hundred dollars at two percent, compounded, and John had been bored by it, had thought the numbers too small to matter. Now the same arithmetic was standing in front of him wearing Flavie's jacket. He didn't want to pontificate the way Mathys did, laying words over people like tarps. But he also couldn't stand there and let her walk to Delmore Street.

"If you renew it, you pay the forty-five again," he said. "Every two weeks. Your mom's check is three weeks out. You'd already be into a second round before she sees a dime. And if she's short again next month, it stacks."

"I can do math," Flavie said, not unkindly. She gave the phone back. "I just didn't know the number was that. Nobody posts almost four hundred percent on a window."

"They post the fifteen," Mathys said, quieter now. "That's the trick, I guess." He looked at the sticker on the coupe, the honest little 5.9%, and John understood they were both recalibrating, the way you do when a scale turns out to be wrong and every weight you ever trusted has to be redone.

"I could ask Ms. Toussaint," Flavie said. "She lent the drama club the bus money once, out of her own pocket, and never said a word about it to anyone. I only know because I saw the receipt."

"She'd say yes," John said.

"I know she would. That's the part that's hard." Flavie looked across the showroom at John's mother, who was shaking the salesman's hand, keys in her other fist. "Borrowing from people who care about you costs something that isn't money."

Across the room his mother waved him over, holding up the keys. He waved back but didn't move yet, and neither did Flavie.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
story:
The email arrived at 4:52 on a Thursday, while Hannah was waiting for her latte at the counter of the coffee shop on Delancey. From: Office of Undergraduate Admissions. Subject: Your Early Action Decision. She read the first line standing up, one hand still reaching for the cup the barista held out to her, and then she had to sit down at the nearest table because her knees had gone strange.

"Accepted," she said out loud, to nobody. Remy looked up from a physics textbook two seats over, where he'd been camped since three with aHighlighter and a dying laptop.

"You got in? Where? Wait, hold on." He dragged his chair over, scattering a napkin. "Early Action? That's the December one, right?"

"Apparently." She turned her phone face-down on the table, then face-up again, then face-down, a small ritual of not knowing what to do with her hands. "It's real, though. It's them. It's the actual school."

Remy whistled. "So you're done. No more essays. You can burn the Common App."

But Hannah was already frowning at the table, because something about his certainty snagged on something Ms. Takahashi had said in the college office back in October, something about Early Action not being a cage. At the time she'd filed it away as one more piece of admissions trivia, the kind of thing she externalized onto a sticky note and stuck to her mirror and then stopped seeing. She pulled the note out now, flattened it on the wood. Non-binding, it said, in her own handwriting.

"What does that mean, though," Remy said, reading upside down. "Non-binding. Like, they can take it back?"

"No." She turned the note around so he could see it properly. "It means I got in early, but I don't have to go. I can still say no in the spring. I could keep applying other places and decide in April like everyone else." She heard herself say it and felt the fact settle into place, the way a formula does when you finally stop memorizing it and start using it. Early answer, no obligation. Both things at once.

Remy leaned back. "Why would anyone keep applying after getting in? That's insane. That's like finishing a marathon and then running two more for fun."

Jean arrived then, shaking rain off her jacket, and slid into the third chair without asking. "Running two more for fun" was apparently enough context for her, because she caught up in about ten seconds, which was typical. "It's not insane," she said. "It's called keeping your options open. Some people like options." She stole the corner of Hannah's muffin. "Some people are also deeply noncommittal and it ruins their lives, but that's a separate issue."

"That's exactly the issue," Hannah said, quieter than she meant to. Because it was true that she had been noncommittal about everything lately, the college list, the second semester electives, whether to keep playing cello, and she had told herself it was carefulness, open-mindedness, a willingness to weigh competing goods. But sitting here with an acceptance in her pocket and eleven unfinished supplements due in twelve days, she had to admit the other possibility: that she had been avoiding choosing anything at all.

"Okay," Jean said, "but here's the thing about you. You do this thing where you treat every decision like it's enthalpy, like there's some hidden energy cost you have to calculate before you're allowed to react. You got into a school you actually like. You're allowed to just be happy for one evening without solving it."

Remy raised his mug to that. Hannah laughed despite herself, and then sat with it, the three positions arranged in front of her like exhibits: Remy saying the acceptance was an ending, Jean saying it was a feeling to have, and the sticky note saying it was neither, just a door propped open. She didn't have to decide tonight whether to finish the other applications. She only had to decide whether to keep them possible, and that was smaller, that she could do.

"Remy," she said, "do you still have that list of schools with January deadlines?"

He pulled a crumpled printout from his backpack, and she smoothed it flat next to the sticky note, and picked up her latte, which had gone warm but not cold. "One essay tonight," she said. "The bad one, for the school I'll probably never go to. Just to see if I still want the option." She opened her laptop and the cursor blinked in the empty document, waiting.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
The planetarium smelled like dust and old carpet, and the dome above the folding chairs was still gray, waiting to become a sky. Anna sat in the back row with the Mauna Loa graph printed on a sheet of paper that had gone soft at the corners from handling. In two days she would have to stand under the projected stars and explain, to a room of parents and younger students, how greenhouse gases trapped heat, and she did not yet understand the paper in her hands.

The line climbed from left to right, decade over decade, and that part she could explain. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured at a station on a volcano in Hawaii, rising and rising. What she could not explain was the way it shuddered. Every year the line jumped up, then dropped down, then jumped again, a sawtooth underneath the climb, as if the instrument at Mauna Loa were flinching. She had decided, privately, that the wiggles were noise. Measurement error. She would draw a smooth average over them in marker and never mention it.

Alix dropped into the seat beside her, boots clacking on the tiered floor, and stole one of the mints Anna kept in her jacket pocket. "You look like the graph personally insulted you."

"It did, kind of." Anna flattened the page against her knee. "This part. The little zigzags. I think they're mistakes."

Alix leaned over, chewing, and looked for a long moment. Then she said, "What happens to trees in spring?" Anna blinked at her. "I'm serious. Like, all the trees. What do they do?"

Before Anna could answer, the dome went black, and then it was not black anymore. The projector hummed somewhere below them, and stars bloomed across the ceiling in a slow wheel, and Amara, two rows down, said "oh" in a hushed voice, transfixed. Anna kept her eyes on the paper in her lap, the way the light from the screen made it glow faintly blue.

Plants grow in spring and summer, she was thinking. Northern Hemisphere plants, most of the world's land and most of its forests. They take in carbon dioxide as they grow, pulling it out of the air, and the line at Mauna Loa dips. Then autumn comes, and the leaves die and decay, and the carbon goes back into the air, and the line climbs again. It was not noise. It was the planet breathing, one breath per year, recorded in ink. The wiggles were seasons. She felt something shift in her, small and seismic at once, the ground under an assumption moving.

Mr. Gupta's voice came through the dark from the front, low, telling the younger students to find the North Star. He was the one who had assigned this. Anna raised her hand anyway, out of habit, though he could not see her. Amara turned around in her seat.

"What," Amara whispered.

"It's not an error." Anna's voice came out louder than she meant. "The zigzags. It's plants. Every spring and summer, plants take in carbon dioxide while they grow, and in autumn and winter the leaves die and decay and release it. That's the sawtooth. The whole Northern Hemisphere, breathing."

Alix sat back slowly. "That's what I was getting at, yeah."

"You could have just said the whole thing."

"You were the one who called it a mistake." Alix took another mint, unrepentant.

When the lights came up, Mr. Gupta walked the tiers collecting questions on index cards, and Anna looked at her graph differently now. The climb was still there, still the same climb, and underneath it the breathing, and both were true at once. She had wanted the data to be one story, clean, a single line with a single villain. It was two stories braided together, the world's annual rhythm and the thing humans had done to it, and she would have to say both out loud on Saturday without flattening either one.

"I still don't know how to say the scary part," Amara said, coming up the aisle with her own graph rolled like a baton. "The heat-trapping part. My cousin says there's no point caring about anything anyway. Full nihilism. He says the ocean's cooked whether I explain it or not."

"That's not a reason not to explain it," Anna said. "That's just him being tired."

They stood in the lobby while the younger students filed out into the afternoon light. Anna folded her graph along the zigzag, then unfolded it, then folded it again into a small square that fit in her palm. The projector behind them was still running; through the half-open door she could hear the hum, and a sliver of stars lay across the carpet, warped by the doorframe, sliding as the sky wheeled.

"So Saturday," Alix said. "You open with the breathing, and then?"

Anna looked down at the square of paper in her hand, the whole record of a century folded small enough to lose. "Then the climb."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and hot plastic chairs, and Sarah sat in the third row of graduates with her speech folded into quarters inside her gown pocket. She had written it twice. The first version had been about doors opening, which the principal had praised and which she could not now read without wincing. The second version was folded in her other pocket, and she had eleven rows of processing left to decide between them.

The band started up, and the seniors rose in the order Ms. Goh had drilled into them that morning. "Slow steps," Ms. Goh had said, standing on a folded gym mat in her conference blazer. "You are not being chased." Now Sarah walked the perimeter of the basketball court under the sting of the processional, and behind her Lukas whispered, "Every graduation in every movie, this song. I swear it's the law."

"I know where it's from," Hunter said, two chairs over, not whispering at all. "Othello. We did it in English."

"Othello the tragedy," Sarah said. "That's a graduation song."

"The title," Hunter said. "Elgar took the title from Othello."

Sarah filed this away the way she filed most things Hunter said, which was sideways and with suspicion, and took her seat. But the music kept going, verse after verse, patient and solemn, and she found herself running the phrase through her head. She mouthed it under the principal's welcome: pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. Othello saying goodbye to the only life he understood. She had written an essay on that speech in October, arguing that Othello knew exactly what story he was telling even as he told it falsely.

The principal's remarks took fourteen minutes and contained the word "journey" nine times. Sarah counted. Beside her, Lukas verbalized his review of it in a single exhale through his teeth. Ms. Goh, stationed at the edge of the stage, caught the sound and looked at them with an expression that could have been pride.

Sarah unfolded the second speech under the program on her lap. She had written it after finding the Othello connection herself, late, in the school library, with a reference book open on her knees. It argued that they were marching in to a piece of music named after the pride and circumstance of glorious war, and that Elgar had lifted the title from a play about a man undone by believing the wrong story about someone he loved, and that maybe the honest thing was to admit they did not yet know which stories about themselves were false. It was a better speech. It was also, she suspected, a speech that would land in a gymnasium of relatives like a stone in a shallow pond, and her mother was in the fifth row of bleachers holding her phone sideways.

The trouble was that both speeches were true. Doors were opening; that was not a lie just because it was a cliché. And the music did mean the thing Hunter said it meant, and pretending otherwise felt like a small, cheap dishonesty that she was apparently willing to commit for the comfort of two hundred aunts. She could not verbalize the difference between a kindness and a cowardice, and she had tried, out loud, alone in her room, until the words turned to mud. Choosing felt like stepping into a quagmire either way: one sank slowly in pleasant language, or quickly in front of everyone.

"Graduates," the principal said, "we come now to the student address."

Sarah stood. The folding chairs scraped. Somewhere behind her a baby made a sound like a hinge, and the air conditioning rattled in the ducts overhead, and the floor under her flat shoes had a faint alluvial softness, silt-fine dust of a thousand games ground into the varnish. She walked to the podium and found, under the lights, that she could not see her mother's face at all, only the general shape of the bleachers, which made it easier.

She put the first speech, the safe one, on the podium. Then she took out the second one and laid it beside the first, side by side, and looked at them for a moment that lasted longer than she intended.

"So," she said into the microphone. "The song we walked in to. Does anybody know where the title comes from?"

Lukas, in the third row, raised his hand.

fact: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula; for carbon dioxide it is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, or 44.01 grams per mole.
story:
The chemistry outreach day at the science museum ended with a competition, and the prize was a guaranteed spot in the summer lab intensive, the one Kevin had been told was already full. He found this out from a flyer taped to the marble near the ticket counter, and he read it twice, because he had been told a lot of things lately that turned out to be negotiable.

"It's rigged," said Jeremiah, who had come along mostly for the planetarium and the vending machines. "They disenfranchise guys like us by making the entry fee ten dollars."

"The entry fee is a pencil," said Johnny. "You have a pencil."

Mr. García, who ran the outreach program, handed out the problem sheets at a long table under the pendulum. The pendulum swung in its patient arc overhead, knocking down one little peg every few minutes, and Kevin kept glancing up at it as if it might knock down his chances too. The problem on the sheet gave a mass of carbon and asked for the moles of carbon dioxide formed, which meant converting through molar mass, which meant Kevin had to remember how to build the number himself.

He worked fast, tongue between his teeth. Carbon, 12.01. Oxygen, 16.00. He wrote 12.01 plus 16.00, got 28.01, and started down the page with the easy momentum of a boy who believes he is done. Jeremiah, beside him, was still drawing a tiny skull on the corner of his sheet and had not opened his pencil case.

"Wait," Kevin said, mostly to himself. "There's two of them."

"Two of what?" Jeremiah said.

"Oxygens. Carbon dioxide. C O two." He looked up at the giant periodic table mounted on the wall behind Mr. García's table, a mural of colored tiles, and found oxygen in its square, 16.00 printed in the corner like a price tag. He wrote it again, doubled it, 32.00, and added it to the 12.01. "Forty-four point oh one."

"That's the molar mass," Johnny said, leaning over from the next seat. "Forty-four point oh one grams per mole. My cousin failed a quiz on that once and now he's a roofer, so."

Kevin redid the rest with his heart going quicker than the arithmetic warranted. Divide the given grams of carbon by twelve point oh one to get moles of carbon, assume every mole of carbon became a mole of carbon dioxide, then multiply by nothing further, because the moles matched one to one. When he turned his sheet over he found the second problem, then a third, and he forgot the pendulum entirely.

Afterward the three of them stood at the climate exhibit while Mr. García graded, watching a glass case where dry ice fogged and curled. A placard listed the gas in the case and its molar mass, 44.01 grams per mole, and Kevin felt the small, unreasonable pride of seeing a number he had built with his own pencil standing in public, printed and official.

"Here's my trenchant analysis," said Jeremiah, who had not finished his sheet and did not seem wounded by it. "Carbon dioxide weighs more than the carbon you start with because the oxygens come along for the ride, and nobody pays you for carrying them. It's like an externality. You do the reaction, the oxygens show up on your balance sheet."

"That is not what externality means," said Johnny.

"It's close enough for a vending machine budget."

Mr. García came down the aisle holding the sheets, and he stopped in front of Kevin and tapped the page where the 44.01 sat, circled twice. "You doubled the oxygen," he said. "Half the field forgets. You caught it yourself."

"Almost didn't," Kevin said.

"Almost is where chemistry lives." Mr. García wrote something on his clipboard and did not tell them what it was, which Kevin decided was either very good news or a very efficient way of avoiding bad news. The pendulum knocked over another peg behind them, tick, and started its slow swing back across the room.

"Well?" Jeremiah said.

"Well what?"

"Are you in the summer thing or not?"

Kevin folded the problem sheet into quarters and put it in his back pocket. "He wrote my name down. That's all I know." Jeremiah groaned and Johnny bought three sodas with the money he had saved by not entering, and outside, on the museum steps, Kevin checked his pocket twice to make sure the paper was still there.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: The Framingham Heart Study, which began following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, gave medicine the term 'risk factor' for habits and conditions that raise later disease risk.
story:
The open house had been Parker's idea, though his mother had done most of the driving, and now she was three tables away at the financial aid booth while he stood in front of a display for the Department of Epidemiology, wondering whether anyone would notice if he just left. The banner above the table read PUBLIC HEALTH: THE SCIENCE OF POPULATIONS, and beneath it a graduate student was arranging pamphlets into a fan, the way people do when they have nothing else to do.

"You look like someone with a question," she said. Her name tag read MYLA, and she was wearing a lanyard covered in enamel pins, one of which was a tiny heart.

Parker did have a question, but it wasn't the kind you asked at a table. It was the kind that had been sitting in his chest since March, when his grandfather had driven himself to a checkup and then called from the parking lot, his voice careful in a way Parker had never heard before. "I have to decide," Parker said, "whether to write my enrollment deposit for engineering here, or epidemiology. The deadline's Monday." That much was true. What he left out was that his grandfather had told him, over pancakes last weekend, to take the engineering money, that jobs you could name were safer than jobs you had to explain.

Myla handed him a pamphlet. On the cover was a photograph of a small town, row houses and a church steeple, taken from a hill. "Know what this is?" she asked.

"Somewhere in New England."

"Framingham, Massachusetts. In 1948, researchers started following the residents there, and they never really stopped. Whole town, generation after generation." She tapped the photograph. "That study is where medicine got the term 'risk factor.'"

Parker turned the pamphlet over. There was a timeline inside, dense with small print, but she had already moved on to help a woman asking about prerequisites, so he stood at the edge of the booth and read. The phrase sat strangely in his mind. A factor, like in algebra, something you could isolate. A risk, which sounded like weather, something that arrived at you. His grandfather used to say that his own father had dropped dead at fifty-two shoveling snow, and nobody had called it anything but bad luck and a bad winter.

He found his mother at the financial aid table, filling out a card with her careful, small handwriting. She asked whether he had learned anything, and he said, "They ask about your habits now. Smoking, weight, all of it. Because of a study. They followed one whole town starting in 1948, and now there's a name for the things that raise your chances later. Risk factor." She said that was interesting and looked back at her card.

He wandered into a lecture hall where a sample mini-lecture was starting, given by a professor introduced as Dr. Emie, a small woman who began by writing a single question on the board: HOW DO WE KNOW WHAT WE KNOW ABOUT BODIES? She talked for ten minutes about how numbers collected from thousands of strangers could tell you something about your own particular body, and how the interpreting of those numbers was almost a kind of hermeneutics, reading data like a text, and Parker wrote that word down even though he wasn't sure he'd spelled it right. He thought of his grandfather's file folder of lab results on the kitchen counter, and his grandfather reading them the way he read the racing form, looking for a sign.

Afterward, in the corridor, Parker caught Dr. Emie folding her notes. "My grandfather," he said, and then stopped, because he hadn't planned to say it. "He just found out his numbers are bad. And he's telling me to do engineering because it's safe. But he spent forty years not asking what his habits were doing, because back then nobody asked." The words came faster than he wanted. "I can't fix him by studying this. I know that. It's not some trade."

Dr. Emie considered him. "No," she said. "It's slower than that. And the payoff isn't personal, usually. It's for people you'll never meet, decades out." She smiled slightly. "Most of what we do is ancillary to actual medicine, in a way. We watch. We count. Someone later decides what to do with it." She gathered her bag and left him with that, in the corridor with its terrazzo floor and its bulletin board of smiling undergrads.

Parker sat on the steps outside the hall and called his grandfather. It rang four times, long enough for Parker to watch a tour group cross the quad, all of them seventeen and eighteen, all of them carrying some decision like a stone in a pocket. His grandfather answered, breathless, saying he was in the garden. Parker said he was at the open house, and that he'd learned something, and that he wanted to tell it right this time. "You know how the doctors kept asking about your smoking and your diet?" Parker said. "In 1948, they started following everyone in this town, Framingham, in Massachusetts, and they tracked them for decades. That's where the term 'risk factor' comes from. The habits. The things that raise your chances of getting sick later." There was a pause, and the sound of a trowel being set down on stone.

"Huh," his grandfather said. "Fifty-two years I figured your great-grandfather was just unlucky."

"Grandpa," Parker said, "I'm thinking of changing my deposit."

"Monday's the deadline," his grandfather said. "You sure you want to talk about it now?"

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
The pass died three feet short of Alyssa's stick, and Isabella blew the whistle before the puck even settled. Eight girls in blue practice jerseys reset at the cones, and she watched them do it again, and again the puck wobbled wide, and she understood that the passing drills she'd copied from a coach's manual were going nowhere.

Ms. González had given her this. Two weeks ago the teacher had stopped her in the corridor with a clipboard and said the under-twelves needed someone to run their Tuesday practices, that the regular coach was out with a bad hip. Isabella had said yes before she'd thought it through, which was how most things in her sixteenth year had begun.

"Again," she called. "Bend your wrists. Rotate through the hips."

They bent their wrists. They rotated their hips. The passes stayed ugly, fluttering like wounded birds across the neutral zone, and behind her Malika lowered her voice. "That's the fourth one that went wide. You're telling them the same thing louder."

"I'm telling them the same thing correctly."

"Correctly and usefully aren't the same thing," Malika said, which had the sound of wisdom and, Isabella suspected, was actually specious, something borrowed from a motivational poster. She said so. Malika shrugged and skated off to herd the defensemen.

At the bench during the water break, Isabella scrolled her phone, looking for anything on youth passing drills. She found a study instead, by a researcher named Gabriele Wulf, and stood very still while the cold from the bleachers crept through her gloves. Learners usually improved faster when they were told to focus on the effect of a movement, on something like the target, rather than on their own body parts. She read it twice. She had spent forty minutes saying wrists and hips and elbows, turning these kids' attention inward, toward the machinery of themselves, and the machinery had only gotten louder.

"That's called external focus," Alan said, reading over her shoulder. He'd come to help with the goalies and had clearly been eavesdropping for some time. "The other kind's internal."

"You knew this?"

"I read it for a psych thing. It's not complicated."

It wasn't complicated, which was somehow worse. All her careful instructions, the ones she'd rehearsed in front of her bedroom mirror, had been aimed at the wrong place entirely. She looked out at the rink, where the smallest girl was tapping her stick against the ice in that idle way that could portend either boredom or brilliance, and Isabella made a decision that felt less like sagacity than like jumping.

She called them in and squatted at the edge of the faceoff circle. "Forget your wrists," she said. "Forget all of it. When you pass, I want you to look at your teammate's stick blade. That flat part right there. Put the puck on it. That's all. Puck onto the blade."

They stared at her. The smallest girl frowned. "What about my elbows?"

"Nothing about your elbows. Blade to blade. Go."

The first attempt still missed. The second didn't. By the fifth repetition, pucks were arriving flat and firm, slapping into the curve of the receivers' blades with a sound like a door closing, and Isabella felt something loosen in her chest that she hadn't known was tight. Malika caught her eye across the ice and tipped her helmet, conceding nothing and everything at once.

What Isabella hadn't noticed, in all that watching of wrists and blades, was the woman in the third row of the stands who had arrived twenty minutes ago and had not left. Ms. González sat with her coat folded beside her and a notebook on her knee, and when the last drill ended and the girls skated their cooldown laps, she came down the stairs with the deliberate pace of someone who had already made up her mind.

"The head coaching job for the under-fifteens comes open in the fall," Ms. González said. "Paid. Real. I needed to see how you handled a session that wasn't working."

Isabella's mouth went dry. "You watched me get it wrong for half an hour."

"I watched you notice," Ms. González said, "and I watched you change. Most people only do the first one." She closed the notebook. "There's a tryout squad in September. Think about whether you want it."

Then she was walking toward the exit, and Isabella stood at the boards with the Zamboni already rumbling at the far gate, not knowing yet what she would say, her stick tapping once against the ice.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
Isla had learned the opening of the song in three days, and she had spent the following two weeks playing it. The chords sat under her fingers like a path worn through grass, and every evening after dinner she took the guitar to her room, propped one heel on the bed frame, and let the intro unspool, six bars, then the little run she'd taught herself, then back to the top. Her mother called it nice through the wall. Isla thought so too, which was exactly the problem, though she didn't know that yet.

The trouble surfaced on Saturday, when Rio came over to trade songs the way they had since September. He asked for the whole piece, and when she got to bar nineteen her left hand simply stopped. The F shape that had felt impossible in October still felt impossible, and worse, invisible, because she had been circling it for weeks without ever landing on it. Rio watched her restart twice, then asked why she kept beginning at the beginning when the beginning was the only part she could already do.

She said the beginning was the fun part, and he said sure, and neither of them argued. But after he left she sat on the bed with the guitar flat across her knees, wondering whether fun and getting better were two directions from the same door. She had been thinking of practice as a kind of accumulation, hours in, songs out. The evidence of the evening suggested something less flattering: that she had spent two weeks preserving what she had and calling it growth.

On Monday she walked to the library branch near the shops and exhumed a book on learning from the shelf marked education, a thick, dusty thing nobody had signed out since before she was born. She skimmed past chapters about talent and genius until she found a chapter that described what researchers called deliberate practice. It was a strange pairing of words, deliberate and practice, as if implying that most practice happened without deliberation, which was suddenly and personally accurate. She read the page twice on the bench outside, then photographed it.

The idea was narrow and almost disappointingly plain. Working on specific weaknesses, with a clear goal for each attempt, and feedback that arrived immediately, improved skill more than simply playing through pieces already known. She tested the sentence against her own evenings like a key against a lock. Her weakness had a name and a bar number. Her goal had been nothing, or worse, the vague wish that bar nineteen would fix itself. Her feedback had been muffled by the pleasant wash of the six bars before it.

That night she made a deal with herself, and she broke it within four minutes, because starting at bar nineteen felt like pressing on a bruise. She caught herself back at the intro, that easy pleasure, and noticed how quickly her hands had wandered home without asking her. It was a small peccadillo, really, the craving to sound good to herself, but she wrote it on a sticky note anyway, put the note on the amp, and dragged the music stand to face the wall so the sheet was only bar nineteen and twenty, nothing ancillary, no intro to retreat into.

She set a timer for ten minutes and a rule: play the two bars, stop, listen, adjust, again. The first minute produced only the sound of her failure, which was instructive in a way the intro had never been. The second finger of her left hand was landing a half-beat late, every single time, and without the six comfortable bars to disguise it, the lateness stood there and admitted itself. She fixed one thing, then chose the next, the buzz on the top string, and after nine minutes she could hear the chord change, imperfect but arriving on time, and she felt something she couldn't yet name, closer to recognition than triumph.

Bryan came by on Thursday, and she told him she wasn't going to play him the song. He looked disappointed until she explained what she was doing instead, and then he asked whether it wasn't boring, drilling two bars like that. She started to say no, then stopped, because honestly she didn't know. It was boring the way a microscope was boring, and it was interesting the same way, depending on whether you wanted the thing under the lens. He picked up her sticky note, read her handwriting about sounding good to herself, and put it back without comment.

She still played the intro, some nights, for the pleasure of it, and she had decided this was allowed. What she hadn't decided was where the line lived between loving a thing and using it as a hiding place, whether an hour of honest difficulty outweighed an evening of comfort, or whether the comfort was part of why she'd wanted the guitar at all. On Friday she stood in front of the mirror with the fretboard visible and played bars nineteen and twenty to her own reflection, watching her fingers in the glass, listening for the buzz. On the third pass it was clean, and she let the chord ring out and held it there, both hands still, counting the seconds until it faded.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
Michael was on his knees in the pavilion at Riverside Park, pressing his thumb into a line of small clay cups to steady them, when his aunt handed him the bag of cotton wicks and said the guests would start arriving within the hour. His cousins had absconded to the playground the moment the tables were carried in, and his mother had gone back to the car for the third box of sweets, so the rows fell to him and to his aunt, who moved along the edge of the pavilion placing each little lamp with a precision he had learned not to disturb. He dipped the wicks in oil, set one in each cup, and tried to keep them from touching, because a wick that leaned against the clay burned crooked and drowned.

It was the first year the celebration had been moved to the park. For as long as Michael could remember it had happened in his grandmother's house, every window crowded with the small flames, and last year he had spent the whole evening in the kitchen on his phone while his grandmother stood alone at the door handing sweets to neighbours. He had told himself he was tired. He was not sure he believed that anymore, and the thought arrived now the way inconvenient thoughts did, in the middle of a task, while his hands were too busy to push it away.

He heard Trace before he saw him, the particular rattle of his skateboard over the park's cracked path. Trace and Mika came up the slope with the board under Trace's arm, and Mika was already saying something about the floodlit courts on the other side of the park, where a dozen people were gathering for the evening. "You said you might come after," Trace said, which was true in a limited sense; Michael had said it two weeks ago, before he knew he would be here until dark, and had never corrected it.

"I can't," Michael said. "I've got all this to finish before people show up."

Mika crouched at the edge of the nearest row. "My grandmother does these," she said, touching the rim of one of the little lamps. "We're Jain. I always thought it was just us, honestly, and then just Hindu friends at school. Then my cousin married a Sikh guy and their houses look the same at this time of year."

"They're called diyas," Michael's aunt said over her shoulder, without pausing in her circuit of the pavilion. She said it the way she said most things, as though offering a fact that could be taken or left.

"Even some Buddhists keep them," Mika said, mostly to herself, turning the clay cup so the wick faced the last of the daylight.

Michael lit the first row with the long match his aunt had left him, and the wind off the river took two of the flames immediately. He cupped his hands around the third and held them there until the flame steadied, and while he knelt in that awkward posture he found himself telling the friends, in a low voice, that he had not wanted to come tonight. That last year he had stayed in the kitchen at his grandmother's. Trace looked at the ground. Mika looked at the lamps.

"She knew," Michael said. "She never said anything. She just kept bringing me sweets."

The subtext of the evening, he understood slowly, was not about lamps at all. His grandmother had kept lighting hers whether he watched or not; his aunt had kept setting them out whether the celebration filled a house or a rented pavilion; the small flames were meant to stand for light overcoming darkness, and that was all they were asked to do, without guarantee of who noticed. Michael had been building some inchoate theory of obligation all afternoon, that duty was a thing owed to the dead and the living in equal, unmeasurable parts, and he could not make the arithmetic work. What he did have was a match, a row of unlit cups, and two friends who had not left.

"Stay and light one," he said. "Then we can all go to the courts for a while before the guests come."

Trace set the skateboard down against a table leg. Mika picked up a match, and the three of them moved down the row together, shielding each new flame from the wind with their jackets, one lamp catching from another. By the time his mother came back across the grass carrying the box of sweets, the whole pavilion edge was burning, small and steady, and Michael stood back and looked at the length of it, the light running out further than he had planned for.

"That one's yours," he said to Trace, pointing at the lamp nearest the river, the one that had almost gone out twice.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, so today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after.
story:
Cameron had agreed to the camping trip before he remembered the presentation, and by then it was too late to remonstrate with Manuel, who had already packed the tent, the stove, and a printout of their assignment in the same duffel bag. The assignment was due Monday. They were two hours from school, sitting on a granite shelf above the lake, and Ms. Nkosi's note was still folded in Cameron's pocket: Build a prediction from the pyramid. Defend it.

"Here," Manuel said, smoothing the printout on a flat stone. It was a population pyramid of a town they had invented for the exercise, mostly because real data was harder to argue with. The bars spread wide at the bottom, narrow in the middle, wide again at the top. Laurianne leaned over from her camp chair, a foil packet of instant noodles steaming in her hands.

"The question is the high school," Cameron said. "Ms. Nkosi wants us to say when the town needs more classrooms and when it needs the other thing."

"Nursing homes," Laurianne said. "That's the trade she keeps talking about. Schools or nursing homes, depending which end of the pyramid is fat." She blew on her noodles. The lake made its small evening sounds, water slapping rock, an oar knocking somewhere against a dock.

Cameron traced the bottom bars with his finger. The widest bar was the youngest, zero to four, thick as his thumb while the others were slimmer. He remembered failing a quiz on this in the spring, drawing arrows that went every direction, and remembered too his father saying, after the grade came home, that a wrong answer you corrected yourself stays corrected. He had not believed it then. He was starting to.

"So these fat bars," Manuel said. "All those babies. They're babies now. What are they in five years?"

Cameron looked at the pyramid again. Five-year age groups, the side of the page said, each bar a band of five years. He put his finger on the bottom bar and slid it up one. "They're the next bar. In five years all of them are five to nine. Then in another five they're ten to fourteen." The bulge didn't spread out or shrink as he moved it; it just climbed, one bar at a time, like something ascending stairs. "A bulge moves up one bar every five years," he said slowly, testing the sentence as he said it.

"So count the bars," Laurianne said. "How many fives until they're us."

He counted. The bottom bar, then two more, and then the bar that held fourteen to eighteen year olds, the high school bar, thin right now, obviously thin, because the printout showed a town with an old high school and empty classrooms. Three moves up, one every five years. He said the number out loud and Manuel laughed, one sharp syllable, and started stacking twigs for the fire.

"That's the whole presentation," Manuel said. "Big group of babies today, big group of high schoolers in fifteen years. Build the wing now." He lit the kindling, and the smoke bent toward the lake with the breeze.

Cameron was not sure it was that simple, and he said so. There were things the pyramid did not show, whether families would stay or leave, whether the town would vote for the money, whether a prediction was the same as a plan. Laurianne called that the metaphysics of bar charts, and he had to admit the phrase was fair. But a prediction he could defend, a tenable one, was worth more to him than a certainty he could not. He got out his notebook and began sketching the pyramid freehand, arrows moving up the bars one step at a time, while the fire took hold and Manuel arranged three foil packets along the coals.

"You're drawing in the dark," Laurianne said.

"There's still light." He tilted the page toward the last of it, the sky gone the color of the cooling stove, and added one more arrow, rising.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
Zachary's grandmother had turned her back sunroom into a reading room, and on the first Sunday of October it held four chairs, a plate of shortbread, and the paperback copies of Jane Eyre that Mr. Jean-Louis had lent out in September. The book club was supposed to be his grandfather's, but his grandfather had been dead for two years, and somehow the thing had kept meeting, rotating members, and now included Zachary, who had joined only because his mother thought he needed something other than his phone.

"Page ninety," said Mr. Jean-Louis, the retired teacher from across the street, tapping his copy. "Rochester describes Blanche Ingram's family fortune and hers. Read it aloud, Zachary. Slowly."

Zachary read the passage, the one where Jane watches Rochester and Blanche together and calculates, in cold arithmetic, everything she lacks: family, connections, fortune. He kept his voice flat because he'd been practicing a flat voice all week, the voice of a person doing analysis instead of having feelings.

"Now," Mr. Jean-Louis said, "your assignment. Tell us what a Marxist lens sees here."

Helena leaned forward before Zachary could speak. She had come with her own book, a thin dark pamphlet she'd found on the shelf beside the fireplace, and she held it up. "I think we need this first." She opened it and read, "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles." She looked around the room. "That's the first line of the first section. It's from the Communist Manifesto, Marx and Engels, 1848. I found it with your grandfather's things, Zachary. Does it fit the novel?"

Zachary felt the room tilt slightly. His grandfather, who had owned a hardware store for forty years and once remonstrated with a city inspector for a full afternoon over a permit, had owned a copy of the Manifesto, and had apparently read it enough that its spine was cracked. He put that aside, because the question was a real one and he had prepared for a version of it.

"Okay," he said. "If that line is true, then Jane isn't just sad at a party. She's a governess. She works for her living inside a house she can never belong to. Rochester can marry Blanche because Blanche's family has money that matches his. Jane's feelings don't matter to that machinery at all. So when she says she has no fortune, that's not self-pity, it's her stating her exact position in the structure." He paused. "But here's my problem with it. When Jane finally tells Rochester she loves him, the book treats it like a soul speaking to a soul. And when the inheritance comes, the plot solves the class problem by giving Jane money of her own, which almost proves the Marxist point and almost refutes it, and I can't decide which."

"Decide," said Carolyn, who was eighteen and had opinions the way other people had pulse rates. "You can't just sit on the fence. Either the novel is conservative or it's radical. Pick."

"It's both, and I don't think picking is honest." He heard how prim that sounded and pushed on anyway. "Charlotte Brontë was writing in 1847, a year before that manifesto. She wasn't answering Marx. She was writing what she saw. What she saw was a woman with nothing but her own mind, and the novel gives that mind a voice so vitriolic about injustice that people at the time called it coarse. And it also lets the happy ending arrive only once the money question is settled. Both of those are in the book. I trust the book more than I trust my lens."

Helena turned the pamphlet over in her hands. "Your grandfather underlined that line," she said quietly. "And about thirty others. In pencil."

"Underlined it agreeing or disagreeing?" Zachary asked.

"That," said Mr. Jean-Louis, "is exactly the right question, and it is unanswerable, which is also, I suspect, the lesson of your paper." He took a piece of shortbread and ate it, which was his way of closing a discussion.

Zachary looked at the pamphlet in Helena's hands, at the penciled line running under the words about class struggles, and thought about his grandfather's probity, the thing neighbors still mentioned at the store, that he never once cheated a customer on a measurement or a price. A man like that, underlining that line. Either he had found in it a description of the world he quietly served every day, or a warning against something, and there was no one left to ask.

"Can I see it?" he said.

Helena passed it across the table. Zachary held it open to the first page and read the line again to himself, and at the bottom margin, small and slanted, he found one more pencil mark, an arrow beside three words his grandfather had written there, and he lifted the book toward the window light to read them.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
The bus shelter's scratched ad for the restaurant had been looking at Nathaniel for three weeks before he did anything about it, a photograph of a stack of pancakes that seemed to portend a life with money in it, his own money, forty hours of summer wages nobody could audit. Hassan had applied first and been hired in two days, which was either encouragement or a dare. "It's not a big deal," Hassan kept saying, in the tone people use for things that are exactly a big deal. "Ms. Brown just talks to you. Like a person."

Nathaniel did not believe interviews worked that way. Interviews, as far as he could tell from the internet, were performances graded on hidden rubrics, and the internet had opinions about how to pass them. He sat at his bedroom desk the night before with a notebook open to a page headed "group project," which was the only story he had, and it was not a good one. In tenth grade he and Musa and two others had been assigned a presentation on water rights, and Nathaniel had taken over the whole thing, redone everyone's slides at midnight, and Musa had stopped speaking to him for a month. That was the story of his life so far, apparently, and now he had to sell it.

"Here, look at this," Hassan said at lunch, leaning over with his phone. "It's called the STAR method." He scrolled while Musa watched with the flat attention of someone waiting to be insulted. "You answer interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result. That's it. Situation, Task, Action, Result." Hassan said it the way he explained plays in the huddle, quick and certain, and Nathaniel copied the four words into his notebook and underlined them twice.

Musa looked at the page for a long moment. "So you take the worst thing you did and you format it." He was not smiling. "That project, you mean the one where you did my part without asking."

"I redid your part," Nathaniel said. "It was bad and I fixed it."

"It was bad because I'd been up all night and I told you that, and you fixed it anyway." Musa pushed his tray half an inch away, a small deliberate gesture, and Nathaniel felt the shape of the thing he had been carrying around for a year without naming it. He wrote STAR in the margin and did not write anything under it.

The restaurant smelled like syrup and burnt coffee, and at four in the afternoon it was nearly empty, one old man reading a paper by the window. Ms. Brown turned out to be the manager, a woman in her fifties with a pen behind her ear, and she sat him in a booth instead of at the counter, which unsettled his whole imagined geometry of the interview. She asked the expected question, almost word for word as the internet had promised: tell me about a time you worked with a team and something went wrong.

He had the answer prepared. Situation, Task, Action, Result, and he began it, laying the water rights project out in four clean moves, and it sounded like a lab report. Somewhere in the middle of the Action he heard himself and stopped, because the Action he was describing was not the action he had taken. In the prepared version, he had "communicated concerns and stepped up to support the team." What he had actually done was decide, alone, at midnight, that Musa's exhaustion did not matter as much as the grade. Ms. Brown's pen was poised over her notepad. "That's the version I practiced," he said. "Do you want the real one?"

She set the pen down. "The real one."

So he told it plainly: the Situation, the group failing apart; the Task, a presentation due in six days; the Action, taking over everything without asking, because it was faster and because, honestly, he thought he was right; the Result, an A on the project and a friendship that had gone quiet for most of a semester. "The method is good," he said, feeling his way through it. "It made me see there was a Result at all. I'd only ever counted the grade. But the same story in the same order can be the truth or a kind of lie, depending on what you admit in the Action." He hadn't planned to say that. It came out anyway.

Ms. Brown wrote something short on her notepad. "You know what I watch for?" she said. "People who've never been wrong on purpose. Sunday morning we get slammed, church crowd, munificent tippers but unforgiving if the eggs are cold. I need somebody who notices when he's steamrolled someone, before the person's standing there hurt. Hassan said you were like that. Said you'd been trying to say something to Musa since tenth grade and hadn't managed it yet."

"He said that."

"He also said you do the dishes at his house without being asked, which I understand from his mother makes you something of an iconoclast in this town." She almost smiled. "Training Saturday at eight. Bring the shirt they give you, wear the shoes they give you, and if Musa wants an application, tell him we're hiring."

Nathaniel stood, shook her hand because it seemed like the thing to do, and walked out past the old man and the syrup smell into the parking lot, where he got his phone out and looked at it for a while before typing. He settled on: got the job. training saturday. also theyre hiring if you want it. Then he added a second message before he could take it back: the project. i should have asked you first. i knew that then and i did it anyway. He stood under the buzzing sign watching the three dots appear, disappear, and appear again.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Justine had spent the drive to the rink trying to parametrize the evening in advance, which she knew was ridiculous, but she did it anyway: the possible selves she could be, sorted by how much talking each one required. The quiet version was safest. The funny version was a gamble. She parked next to Kaden's bike and went in still undecided, her skates swinging from her shoulder by their laces.

He was waiting by the concession window with two large hot chocolates, and he looked so pleased with himself for having bought them that Justine felt her stomach unknot slightly. Then a small boy in a hockey jersey clipped him from behind, and the hotter of the two cups flipped off the ledge and burst across the floor in a brown wave that reached the laces of Justine's boots. Kaden stood there holding the survivor, his ears going red.

"That's it," he said. "I've ruined it. Ten minutes in and I've thrown hot chocolate at you."

"You threw it at the floor," Justine said. "Near me. Adjacent to me."

"You know what I mean. You've been planning to leave since it happened. I can tell."

She hadn't been, actually, and the unfairness of it made her speak before she could choose a self. "There was this experiment," she said. "In 1966. Elliot Aronson and some colleagues. People watched a quiz show contestant who was really competent, and then he spilled a cup of coffee, and afterward they rated him more likable. It's called the pratfall effect."

Kaden looked at the puddle, then at her. "You made that up to be nice."

"I don't have the imagination. I read it in my brother's psych textbook over winter break because we lost internet for four days." That earned the first real laugh of the night, which was unfortunately at her expense, but she decided to bank it anyway.

They skated badly together for an hour, which was its own kind of pratfall, arms pinwheeling, gripping the boards near the Zamboni gate. Justine was reticent by nature on first meetings, but every time Kaden fell, he narrated it, some running commentary of disgrace, and she kept laughing, and it occurred to her that her plan for the evening had been a kind of asceticism, this strict fasting from any risk of looking stupid, and that the fast was over for both of them. She tested the theory deliberately once, announcing a turn she then missed entirely, and Kaden caught her elbow and said, "See, the pratfall effect," like he'd invented it.

Then he got confident. At the concession window again, refueling, he staged a second spill, nudging his cup toward the edge of the counter with theatrical carelessness while watching her face instead of the cup, and it went over in a slow, obviously voluntary motion, and he stood there waiting to be liked.

"That one doesn't count," Justine said. "You did that on purpose. It only worked for the contestant because nobody could tell." She wasn't entirely sure that was the whole reason, and she said so, because lying smoothly to him seemed worse than admitting the edges of what she knew. "It might also matter that he was competent first. Maybe you can't fake it. Maybe I'm wrong and it's something else entirely about who's watching."

Kaden mopped at the counter with a stack of napkins, thinking. "So the honest version of me is only more likable if it happens by accident."

"I don't know," Justine said. "That's the actual answer, sorry. I'm sixteen and I read one textbook."

He laughed again, not at her this time, and held out the last dry napkin as if presenting evidence. "Okay. Then stop planning and fall down on purpose but pretend it wasn't on purpose, but don't tell me which, and I won't tell you either."

"That is the worst experiment I've ever heard of."

"Race you to the far goal line," he said, and pushed off, and Justine, unraveled laces and all, went after him.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: The 'file drawer problem', a term coined by psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979, describes studies with null results going unpublished, which makes the published record look more positive than the evidence.
story:
Jeremy had chosen the two articles because they disagreed, which was the assignment: find two scholarly pieces on the same question and write a critical review that weighed them against each other. The question he had picked, after twenty minutes of scrolling through the library database, was whether planted buffer strips reduced nitrogen runoff into littoral wetlands. The first article, from a big agricultural journal, said they did, impressively. The second article, from a smaller one, said they did too, slightly less impressively. He sat at the corner table on the second floor with both PDFs open side by side and the uncomfortable feeling that he had accidentally chosen two articles that agreed.

"It's supposed to be a comparison," he said to Faith, who had claimed the chair across from him an hour ago and was highlighting her own reading in a color she called celery. "Mine just... corroborate."

"Then compare how they corroborate." She didn't look up. "That's what Kolton's doing. He found two articles about sleep and screens and he's just going to argue for whichever one lets him stay up."

"That's not a review, that's a wish."

Faith set down her highlighter. She had been his lab partner since sophomore year, the year of the vinegar volcano that Mr. Augustin still brought up at open house, and she had a way of pausing before she said something that made him brace. "Does it bug you that every article you found says the same thing? I typed in four different phrasings tonight. Every single result supports the effect. Fourteen articles. Not one says it didn't work."

Jeremy looked at his two PDFs, then at the search page, then at her. "Maybe it just works," he said.

"Maybe," said Faith, and went back to celery.

The library closed at nine, and by eight he had skimmed six more articles, all positive, all moderate in their claims but pointed the same direction, like a row of flags on a windy day. It was Mr. Augustin, shelving returns two aisles over, who ruined everything by being helpful. He had taught Jeremy's chemistry class before moving to reference work, and he wandered past the table, glanced at the screen, and said only, "Interesting. You finding anything that didn't work?" When Jeremy said no, Mr. Augustin nodded slowly, the way he used to nod at a titration that was about to turn pink, and kept walking with his cart.

Jeremy remembered, then, a moment from junior year that he hadn't thought about since. He had run a whole term project on whether music improved memory, and the results had come out as nothing, a flat line, no effect, and he had never written it up. Nobody had told him not to. There had simply been nowhere obvious to put a thing like that, no class contest for the best null result, and so it had gone into a folder on his laptop called "misc" and been quietly true there ever since. He had considered it, at the time, a personal failure of the experiment rather than a fact about the world.

He typed Robert Rosenthal into the database on a hunch assembled from a footnote he'd half noticed, and found a 1979 paper. He read the abstract twice. Then he leaned across the table.

"It's called the file drawer problem," he said. "Rosenthal, 1979."

Faith frowned. "Meaning what?"

"Studies with null results go unpublished. They sit in drawers. So the published record looks more positive than the evidence actually is." He turned the screen toward her. He was aware, saying it, that his whole review had just collapsed and rebuilt itself in the space of one sentence. What he had thought was a comparison of two articles was really a comparison of two articles against a silence he couldn't measure.

"That's such a disincentive," Faith said. "You run the study, it comes out boring, and you don't even get to publish it. So the next person reads fourteen positives and thinks it's settled." She picked up her highlighter again and then put it down. "I was going to write that screen time definitely affects sleep. Kolton was going to write whatever he wanted to be true anyway."

Jeremy opened a blank document. His review, he decided, would still weigh the two articles, their sample sizes and their hedging, but it would also problematize the consensus they belonged to, would say plainly that fourteen published positives might mean the effect was real or might mean the nulls were in drawers, and that a reader could not tell the difference from the record alone. It felt like the first honest thing he had written for school. He got as far as the second paragraph before the overhead lights clicked twice, the nine o'clock signal, and Mr. Augustin appeared at the end of the aisle with his empty cart.

"Find your disagreement?" Mr. Augustin asked.

"No," said Jeremy, closing the laptop. "I found out why I couldn't."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: An 'I-message', popularized by psychologist Thomas Gordon, states the speaker's own concern, such as 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline', instead of accusing the listener with 'you' language.
story:
Sebastian had been volunteering at the community resource office for six weeks when the coordinator, Ms. Chea, handed him the schedule binder and said she needed someone to handle the Wednesday shift reports. It was the closest thing to a promotion the office offered, and he took it the way people take things they did not quite earn, with a nod and a small apology already forming in his throat.

The reports were simple enough, but the schedule was not. Sami, who covered the front desk on Wednesdays, had left early four weeks running, and the missed hours had begun to show up in the attendance log like small cracks in something Sebastian was supposed to be responsible for. He had watched Sami slip out at four instead of five, jacket over one shoulder, always with a wave that seemed to promise an explanation that never came.

Sebastian's first instinct was to write something sharp. He drafted it on the office computer while the radiator ticked and the afternoon light flattened against the filing cabinets. "You keep leaving early. You need to stop." He read it twice, heard it in Sami's voice, and deleted it. It sounded like something a hall monitor would say, and it would accomplish nothing except making Sami defensive before the second sentence.

He had seen Ms. Chea handle a difficult letter that morning, a reply to a landlord who had accused the office of losing his paperwork. Her draft had opened with a clear statement of what the office had done and what it needed, organized in short numbered points, no adjectives doing the work that facts should do. She had read it aloud once to herself, quietly, the way people test whether a sentence can survive being spoken. Sebastian had found himself lingering by the copier longer than the copies required.

Annabelle came in to drop off flyers and found him staring at the blank screen. "Sami again?" she asked, because everyone knew. He showed her the deleted draft. She pulled over the visitor's chair and said her mother, who was a counselor, used this trick where instead of accusing someone you just stated your own concern. "It's called an I-message," she said. "Like, 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline,' instead of 'you keep messing up.'" Sebastian wrote the phrase on a sticky note, then crossed out messing up and wrote leaving early, because accuracy mattered if this was going to work at all.

The email took him three drafts. The first was too stiff, all structure and no warmth. The second was too soft, so full of let me know if this works for you that it apologized for existing. The third began with the concern itself, that he was worried the missed hours would put their grant reporting behind, followed by two numbered points about what had happened and one question about what Sami needed. He reread it the way Ms. Chea had read hers, under his breath, and sent it before he could add anything gratuitous, some little barb disguised as a joke.

Sami's reply arrived that evening, and Sebastian read it twice before showing it to anyone. Sami's mother had been in and out of the hospital since September, and the four o'clock exits were the visiting window, and he had not known how to say it in an office where everyone seemed to have their lives arranged. The email closed with an offer to make up the hours on Saturdays, and a line that Sebastian reread several times: "This was easier to answer than it would have been if you'd yelled at me."

The next Wednesday, Sami stayed until five, and the two of them reorganized the brochure rack while the office emptied out. Sebastian kept thinking about the email he had almost sent, the one built entirely out of the word you, and how certain it had felt while he was writing it, and how wrong. At the same time, a smaller, less comfortable thought worked at him: he had not written the kind version because he was kind. He had written it because the other version hadn't worked, which was a different thing, and he could not decide whether the distinction mattered.

Ms. Chea stopped at the desk on her way out and glanced at the attendance log, which now balanced. "Nice work," she said, and then, gathering her scarf, "The landlord wrote back, by the way. Says we're the most disorganized office he's ever dealt with, and then lists, in numbered points, everything we asked for." She seemed, for a moment, something close to an aesthete admiring an opponent's form. "Professional tone doesn't always mean friendly," she said. "It just means you keep the doors open." Sebastian looked at the balanced log, then at the email still open on the screen, and printed the landlord's letter to read on the bus.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The stadium smelled of fried onions and rain that hadn't fallen yet, and Maria climbed the concrete steps behind her father with the tickets pressed flat in her fist. Ann and Marcus had saved seats three rows from the top, jackets spread across a whole bank of them, and behind them sat Maria's uncle, who had played Sunday league for twenty years and considered this a qualification. The home side needed a win to stay in the cup, and everyone in the section seemed to know it, passing the fact down the rows like a collection plate.

The first half was cautious, both teams probing, and Maria found she could enjoy the geometry of it if she stopped needing goals. Her uncle could not. He coached from his seat, loudly, and when the visiting striker lingered near the far post, clearly beyond the last defender, he shouted that the man was offside and should be carded for it. The referee did nothing. The striker did nothing either, just stood there while the ball rolled harmlessly out for a goal kick, and Maria filed the moment away, uneasy about something she couldn't yet name.

"That's not how it works," Ann said during the interval, unwrapping a chocolate bar she had smuggled in under her hat. "He wasn't doing anything. He was just standing there."

"Standing offside," her uncle insisted, and the argument might have died there if Marcus hadn't asked the actual question, which was what offside actually meant. Maria realized she didn't have a clean answer. She knew the shape of it, the striker past the last defender, the linesman's flag, but not when it counted, and the gap between knowing the shape and knowing the rule bothered her more than her uncle's shouting did.

The second half opened violently, and then came the corner. The home winger bent it in low and hard, a defender missed it entirely, and the striker who had been lurking offside all afternoon, by her uncle's account, stabbed it home at the near post. The stadium rose as one animal. Her uncle stayed seated, palms up, already bellowing offside at the assistant referee, who was jogging back toward halfway with his flag down.

"There's no offside from a corner," Maria said, and heard how strange it sounded to say something so flat in all that noise. But she had read it, months ago, in the rulebook she'd bought when she started refereeing junior games on Saturdays, and it had stuck because it was odd. "Or from a throw-in, or a goal kick." Her uncle turned on her. She kept going, because the other half of it had just surfaced, the half that explained the first half. "And being in an offside position isn't an offence by itself. He only gets penalized when he's involved in active play." The word involved felt clumsy in her mouth but she meant it: touching the ball, interfering, being part of it. Standing was not being part of it.

The goal stood. The replay on the distant screen showed the whole move in its brief encapsulation, the corner, the miss, the finish, and her uncle shook his head and bought her a tea at the kiosk as a kind of concession, which was the closest he came to admitting anything. Marcus kept asking questions and Maria kept answering, and somewhere in that exchange, shouting over the crowd, she felt something she could only call exhilarating, as if knowing a rule the crowd didn't know had made her briefly the most sagacious person in the section, which was ridiculous, and which she enjoyed anyway.

But the game was not finished with the lesson. In the eighty-ninth minute the home keeper punted long, the same striker ran from what the whole section could see was an offside position, took the pass, and scored again. This time the flag went up before the net had settled.
