Her uncle was on his feet demanding justice, and Maria had to be the one to tell him it was the right call, that this time the striker had become involved, that the rule she had used to defend the first goal was the same rule taking this one away. He sat down slowly. The home side was still winning, still through to the next round, and the stadium sang anyway, but Ann was quiet and Marcus was arguing that the rule was arbitrary, and the win that had exhilarated Maria minutes earlier now felt like it had cost her something she couldn't itemize.

Walking out through the crowded tunnels afterward, her father's hand briefly on her shoulder, she understood that she had been right twice tonight about the same rule, once for the goal that counted and once against the goal that didn't, and that being right had won her nothing except her uncle's sulking and Marcus's new conviction that laws were just opinions with flags. She didn't think the rule was arbitrary. She also couldn't say, not cleanly, why standing offside was nothing and running onto the pass was everything, only that the line was drawn somewhere real and the referee had found it. She was still turning it over when they reached the street and Ann tugged her sleeve.

"He's going to email the league, you know," Ann said, nodding at the uncle ahead of them. "About the rules."

"Let him," Maria said. "I'll send him the page number."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass in grams per mole.
story:
The garage smelled of coconut oil and lye, and Brooklyn had taped a hand-lettered sign to the door that read SUDS BY BROOKLYN, ORDERS BY FRIDAY, which was either a promise or a threat depending on how the week went. Ella sat on an overturned milk crate with her chemistry textbook open on her knees, because her mother had decreed that if she was going to fail the midterm, she would at least fail it somewhere other than the couch. Brooklyn measured oil into a pot on a hot plate. Hugh leaned against the workbench, ostensibly to help, actually to watch Brooklyn measure oil into a pot.

"I don't get why I have to know this," Ella said, turning the textbook toward the light. "Moles. Who cares. It's not like anyone weighs out chemicals in real life."

"That's literally what I do," Brooklyn said, not looking up. She set a digital scale on the bench and zeroed it with one insouciant tap. "Lye is a chemical. Too much and the soap burns you. Too little and it turns into grease puddles."

Ella had assumed soap came from a kit, from a shop, from somewhere that wasn't a garage with a dent in the freezer chest. She watched Brooklyn weigh out the white flakes, and something about it snagged on the page in front of her, the way a word you've mispronounced for years suddenly sounds wrong when someone else says it.

"Wait," Ella said. She read the line again. "The number of moles equals the mass in grams divided by the molar mass in grams per mole." She said it out loud, slowly, as if testing whether it would hold weight.

"Congratulations," said Hugh. "You've discovered reading."

But Ella was already dragging the scale toward her end of the bench. "You're doing grams. The book wants grams divided by grams per mole, and that's just grams divided by grams, and the grams cancel, and you're left with moles. It's the same thing you're doing. It's just got a name." She looked up the molar mass of the lye in the back of her textbook, then did the division on the inside cover of her binder, twice, because she had gotten it wrong the first time and only noticed when the answer came out larger than the mass she'd started with. Her stomach dropped, then lifted. She found her error, a misplaced decimal, and corrected it, and the second answer sat there on the page looking small and exact and almost embarrassing in its plainness.

"Do you want to know how many moles you just weighed?" she asked.

"I want to know if it's the right amount," Brooklyn said, but her voice had softened, and she came to stand behind Ella's shoulder, which was as close to admitting interest as she generally got. Hugh drifted over too, though he watched Brooklyn's face rather than the numbers. The garage was quiet except for the hot plate ticking. Ella understood, then, without being able to say it, that the textbook had been telling the truth twice over: once about the arithmetic, and once about the world, that things made of atoms could be counted, that counting them was ordinary, that her own hands could do it.

She had walked into the garage believing chemistry was a language written for other people, people who would go on to laboratories and white coats, while she would go on to a college she hadn't chosen yet and a major she couldn't name. Now the scale read out grams and the textbook read out grams per mole, and the two of them divided into each other like a hinge closing. Maybe the whole subject worked like this, one real object at a time. Or maybe this was the only part that would ever feel solid, and the rest would stay abstract, exam questions she could parse but not believe in. She held both possibilities in her head the way you hold two keys when only one fits a lock, and she did not pretend to know which was which.

"Give me the number," Brooklyn said. "If you can tell me how many moles, I can scale the batch for the Hendricks order, because my aunt's recipe is in moles and I've been interpolating between batches all month and it's making me insane."

Ella slid the binder across the bench, and Brooklyn copied the figure onto the back of a receipt, and her hand was steadier than it had been all afternoon. Hugh began stacking the molds without being asked, arranging them in rows like he was setting a table for someone he wanted to impress.

"You know this is due Friday," Brooklyn said.

"Then I'll be back Thursday," Ella said, and closed the textbook, and carried it out through the side door into the ordinary evening air.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
Austin had already typed the caption, "Everyone needs to see this tonight," when Draven's bedroom door opened and Zakaria came in carrying two energy drinks and his phone in his teeth.

"That the flood video?" Zakaria asked, dropping the cans on the desk. "Draven sent it to me an hour ago."

The video showed a parking garage filling with black water, cars shoving into each other like barges, somebody screaming off camera. It had forty thousand shares. The caption on the post said it was the mill town two counties over, that the levee had failed, that the plant there was putting three hundred people on furlough by morning. Draven's uncle worked at that plant. That was the part that made Austin's thumbs hover over the post button.

"His mom's already calling people," Draven said from the bed, phone pressed to his ear, his voice doing that flat thing it did when he was scared. "Nobody's answering. If this is real, my uncle loses his job, like, this week."

Austin looked at the number in the corner of the screen. Forty-one thousand shares now. It felt like evidence, the way a crowd feels like evidence, everyone running the same direction meaning the direction must be right. He had his thumb on "share" when something Mr. Yoon had said in September drifted back, something about a guy named Caulfield. Austin had half-listened, the way he half-listened to most things that year, but Mr. Yoon had made them repeat the words like a fire drill.

"Wait," Austin said. "SIFT."

Zakaria cracked a can. "What?"

"It's this thing. Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to the original context." He said it fast, from memory, and even he could hear how it sounded, like a rhyme you learn in elementary school. "Just, wait. Thirty seconds."

Draven lowered his phone. "My uncle's plant, Austin."

"One minute." Austin put his thumb down on the video itself instead of the share button and dragged the frame forward until it showed a waterline on a concrete pillar, a street number stencilled above it. He saved the frame, opened a search engine, and dropped the image in. Reverse image search. He'd done it once for a homework thing and felt faintly ridiculous doing it now, in Draven's room, with Zakaria drinking behind him and the fan clicking and the whole internet apparently already certain.

The results loaded slow. Draven's ceiling fan turned overhead and Austin watched it, and the page was still grey, and Zakaria said, "Forty-five thousand shares, man," and Draven said nothing at all, which was worse.

Then the results came up. The first hit was a news site, dated. The same pillar, the same stencilled number, the same waterline. Not this flood. Not this state, not even this decade. The garage had flooded years ago, in a storm with a different name, and somebody had lifted the footage and re-captioned it.

"It's old," Austin said. "The video's real but the flood is old."

Draven sat up. "Show me."

Austin turned the laptop. Draven took it with both hands, the way people take a document they don't want to believe, and read the date twice. Then he called his mother again, and this time the relief in his voice was so plain that Zakaria looked away, as if he'd opened the wrong door.

"So nobody's on furlough?" Zakaria said.

"I don't know. Maybe they are, maybe they aren't. But that video doesn't prove it." Austin pulled his phone back toward himself and looked at his own draft caption, "Everyone needs to see this tonight," which now seemed to portend nothing except forty-one thousand people all certain about the wrong thing. He deleted the caption. The share itself he let sit there, equivocal, neither sent nor unsent, while he scrolled to find whether any actual news outlet had covered the plant. He found one regional story, thin, saying nothing about layoffs, and one that mentioned possible cuts in the fall. Two accounts that didn't agree.

"The problem," Austin said slowly, "is I still don't know about the plant. I only know the video's fake. Stopping the lie isn't the same as knowing the truth." He was surprised by how much that bothered him, that the method gave him an answer and the answer was mostly a fence, not a road.

"Send the thing about the video being old, then," Zakaria said. "At least people stop freaking out."

Austin did. He typed it plainly, linked the original, posted it, and felt the small clean click of a right thing done at small scale. He refreshed once. Two likes.

Draven's mother called back while Draven was in the kitchen, and the news came through the closed door anyway: the plant was fine, the uncle had been asleep this whole time. Zakaria laughed, and Austin laughed, and then his phone buzzed with a share notification, and he opened it to see that his correction was being reposted by a stranger with a new caption of its own, in capitals: "COVER UP. THE LEVEE BROKE AND THEY'RE HIDING IT."

By the time Austin figured out how to report it, it had four hundred shares.

"Well," Zakaria said, watching the number climb. "You tried."

Austin held the phone up so Draven, coming back in with sandwiches, could see it. "Look what they did to my fact."

Draven leaned in, chewed, and read the capital letters twice. "Next time," he said, "maybe just send my uncle a text."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
The cursor blinked in the box marked "Student Tax Information," and Mia moved the mouse in a small circle, the way her mother did when a page refused to load. It was nearly eleven. The state deadline was in six days, and Ms. Bui had told her class in October that the form was not something to leave for the last weekend, though Mia had left it for the last weekend anyway.

"The FAFSA," her mother said, reading from the top of the screen. She pronounced it carefully, fass-fa. "Free Application for Federal Student Aid. Okay. So this is federal."

"Not just federal," Mia said. She had spent the bus ride home reading the state's aid page, scrolling past paragraphs about residency requirements. "The states use it too. And the colleges. It's one form and everybody reads it. If you don't fill it out, you can't get the Pell Grant, you can't get the federal loans, and the college can't give you its own money either."

Her mother pulled a chair up beside her. On the desk, next to the monitor, sat the manila folder of papers she had brought home from the restaurant office: W-2s, the tax return, a pay stub with the week's hours circled in pencil. "So it decides everything."

"It doesn't decide. It just tells them what we have."

Mia typed her Social Security number, then her mother's, then stopped at the question about household size. She counted in her head: herself, her mother, her grandmother. Three. Her uncle had lived with them until March, when he had absconded to his cousin's place in Charlotte without leaving a forwarding address or the two hundred dollars he owed on the electric bill. Whether he still counted in the household felt like a question with a wrong answer either way.

"Put three," her mother said. "He's not here."

"But the tax return says four. They'll see the return."

"Then they'll see he's gone." Her mother's voice stayed flat, but she reached over and squared the folder's edge against the desk, twice. "You want to call somebody at eleven at night and ask about your uncle?"

Mia tabbed back to the state page. In biology they had spent two weeks on symbiosis, mutualism and parasitism, and she kept thinking the FAFSA was something like that: the family and the government each needing something from the other, the form the place where the two of them touched. Except symbiosis assumed both sides benefited, and she wasn't sure yet which kind this was. The Pell Grant was money you didn't pay back. The loans were money you did. Her mother's income sat somewhere near the line where the first turned into the second, and no amount of scrolling told her which side of it they were on.

Her phone lit up on the desk. Brian: did you do the fafsa yet. Then: emanuel says his sister got 6k from the state bc she filed early. Mia typed one-handed while her mother read the tax line off the return: thirty-one thousand, four hundred and something. She didn't finish typing the number to Brian before she deleted it. It wasn't germane to him, and it wasn't his business, and she was surprised by how quickly she had decided that.

"There's a button," her mother said. "Save and exit. Or submit."

"One more page. Assets." Mia's hands were still on the keys. The checking account had eleven hundred dollars in it; her grandmother's name was on that account too, which meant, maybe, that it counted as an asset of the household, or maybe it didn't, and the form's help text said one thing in plain words and another in the fine print beneath.

"Your grandmother keeps her money in that account," her mother said. "It's hers. For the apartment, if anything happens."

"I know."

"So what do we put?"

Mia looked at the empty box. Eleven hundred dollars, three people, six days until the state's own deadline, and one form that every office, state and federal, would read. She thought of Emanuel's sister, six thousand dollars, filed early, and of her uncle's name still sitting on the tax return like a chair no one had moved.

"Eleven hundred," she said. "It's the truth. If they ask about Grandmother, I'll answer that too."

Her mother watched her type it. The little wheel at the top of the browser turned, and turned, and stopped.

"Submitting," Mia said. "It's submitting."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A first-person narrator can report only what that one character sees, knows or chooses to say, while a third-person omniscient narrator can reveal any character's thoughts.
story:
Maya had claimed the window seat at nine that evening with the novel, a legal pad, and the deadline breathing down her neck: Mr. Janssen wanted twelve hundred words on the narrator by first period. The narrator in question, a woman called only the Sister, spent two hundred pages insisting she had never opened the locked gate, and Maya had spent three days believing her.

She could still see Tuesday's class, Mr. Janssen pacing in front of the whiteboard, asking them why they trusted the Sister at all. "She's the one telling you everything you know," he'd said, and then he'd tapped the marker against the board without writing anything, which was somehow worse. Kalli had raised her hand and said the Sister seemed sad, and Maya had nodded along, and only on the bus home had the wrongness of that settled on her. Sad people lie too. Sad people lie especially well, sometimes, because you want to protect them.

She read the gate scene a fourth time in the nook, knees drawn up, the radiator ticking under the window. The Sister reported everything: the cold iron, the gardener's back turned, her own hand hovering at the latch. What she did not report was what the gardener was thinking, or what the child on the far side of the wall wanted, or anything at all beyond the narrow lantern of her own attention. Maya wrote in the margin, the narrator only tells what she sees, knows, or chooses to say, and then sat back, because that felt like something, though she wasn't sure what yet.

Her phone buzzed against the cushion. Kalli: are you done. is it actually due tomorrow. Maya typed back that it was due tomorrow and that she was stuck, and Kalli called within a minute, voice tinny and panicked, saying she'd written six hundred words about how the Sister was mercurial, one minute guilty and the next minute sweet, and Maya said that was a good word but it wasn't the whole problem. "Try this," she said, and explained the thing she'd just scrawled. "She can only tell us what she sees, knows, or chooses to say. That's it. That's the whole box she keeps us in."

"So it's just a limited person talking," Kalli said slowly.

"Right. But if you rewrote it in third person omniscient," Maya said, "the narrator could get into anyone's head. Any character's thoughts, anytime. The gardener, the kid, all of it." She was pacing now, one socked foot on the window seat, the cordless phone wedged against her shoulder. "Try it. Take one page and swap it."

Kalli swore and said fine, and Maya hung up and did the same thing herself, copying the gate scene onto the legal pad and then crossing out every I and my. The Sister became the woman. And then, because omniscient meant she could, Maya added a line about the gardener: he knew about the gate, had always known, and said nothing so that the woman would have to choose. She stared at what she'd written. In first person, that sentence had been impossible. The Sister couldn't have said it, wouldn't have. In this version, it was just there, flat and true, and it changed the color of everything around it.

The strange part was what it did to the trust. Reading the original, Maya had been inside the Sister, folded into her excuses, her careful omissions half invisible the way one's own are. Reading her own rewrite, she stood outside like a witness, and the omissions became visible as holes. Was that why the book felt so unstable? Not because the Sister was dishonest, exactly, but because every single fact arrived filtered through her, and Maya had no way to check any of it against another mind. She thought of her mother describing her father's leaving, years ago, the two versions of that night never agreeing, and how Maya had eventually stopped asking which was true and started asking instead what each of them needed the story to do. She hadn't thought of that in a long time. She wrote a question on the pad, not an answer: does trusting a narrator mean believing facts or believing feelings?

She worked until one in the morning, cutting her rewrite apart, quoting both versions side by side in the essay. At twelve forty Kalli texted a photo of her own attempt, the gardener's inner monologue rendered in furious purple ink, with the message: this is so weird, i know things now i'm not supposed to know, it feels like cheating. Maya laughed out loud in the dark nook and texted back that it wasn't cheating, it was just a different deal with the reader, a whole different set of promises about who knew what.

By one thirty she had a draft that said, more or less, this: the Sister's unreliability was not a lie she told but a limit she couldn't escape, and the author had chosen that limit on purpose, the way you'd choose to cauterize a wound, sealing off every other point of view so the one that remained had to be enough. Maya didn't know yet if that was a real insight or a late-night one that would evaporate by morning, and she left a note at the top of the page saying so, plainly, for her morning self to judge. She saved the file, closed the laptop, and sat a while longer with the novel still open on her knees, the gate scene facing her, the Sister's steady voice running on in her head like a faucet she hadn't quite shut off.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Papers posted on arXiv, the preprint server Paul Ginsparg started in 1991, are checked by moderators for relevance but are not peer reviewed before they appear.
story:
The bus idled outside the physics building while Ms. Demetriou counted heads for the third time, and Tristan used the delay to reread the first page of his science fair report, which sat folded in his jacket pocket like a confession. His claim, the one printed in bold under the hypothesis, rested on a single paper. He had found it at two in the morning in November, felt the ordinary inchoate excitement of a discovery taking shape, and written it down before the excitement could be cross-examined.

"Relax," Marko said, watching him fold and unfold the page. "You won the regional thing. Whatever it says, it worked."

"It worked because nobody checked it," Tristan said. "That's different from it being true."

Rachael, who had come on the trip mainly for the cafeteria rumors, leaned over the seat. "The university people will know. Just ask one of them and stop chewing your sleeve."

Inside, the lab smelled of machine oil and burnt coffee, and a graduate student with chalk on her sleeves walked them past an optical table bristling with mirrors. She was explaining, in the flat tone of someone who had given the tour a hundred times, that the result the group had published last year had failed to replicate in two other labs before a third one, using a different method, finally confirmed part of it. "So was the first paper wrong?" Rachael asked. "No," the grad student said. "It was early. One result is a conversation starter. Ten results are a conversation." Marko wrote that down, apparently for use in future arguments.

During the question period Tristan's hand went up before he had decided what to say. He asked about preprints, because his paper, the one in his pocket, was a preprint, a word he had typed into the citation without fully internalizing what it implied. The grad student nodded like this was the most useful question of the morning. "If it's on arXiv, the preprint server Paul Ginsparg started in 1991, it's been checked by moderators, but only for relevance, not peer review. It hasn't been reviewed before it appeared. Anything on there might be right, might be wrong, might be brilliant, might be nonsense. It's the raw feed." She moved on to someone asking about lasers.

Tristan sat with that. The moderators, he understood now, were gatekeepers of a kind, but the gate they kept was narrow; they sorted the mail without reading the letters. His single source, which he had presented as settled, was at best a conversation starter, and at worst nonsense, and he had built a trophy on it. Ms. Demetriou, drifting past his row, caught the expression on his face and paused. "Something wrong with the tour?" "No," Tristan said. "Something wrong with my bibliography." She looked at him for a moment longer than necessary, and then, instead of the lecture he was bracing for, said only, "The judges are meeting again in March," and kept walking, which was either mercy or a deadline.

At lunch, in a cafeteria where the pasta was presumably somebody's thesis project, the three of them argued about whether Tristan should email the regional committee and retract. "Retract what?" Marko said. "You didn't fake anything. You cited a source." "I cited it like it was the end of the story," Tristan said. "It's not even the beginning. Nobody's repeated it. Nobody's even reviewed it." Rachael stirred her drink. "So your recompense for winning with bad evidence is losing sleep and bad pasta." "It's not recompense if nobody's punishing me," Tristan said. "I'm doing it to myself." "That's the worst kind," Rachael said. "There's no one to apologize to who'll feel better afterward."

The argument did not resolve, which Tristan was beginning to suspect was the natural state of arguments. Marko thought truth was whatever survived the judges; Rachael thought truth was whatever survived the group chat; the grad student, if asked, would probably have said truth was whatever survived three labs and several years. He could hold all three in his head at once without any of them collapsing, and he noticed that this was less comfortable than picking one, and probably more honest. What he could not do was un-know that his prize rested on an unreviewed preprint, and that the difference between a conversation starter and a conversation was the entire difference.

Back in the lab for the afternoon session, the grad student let them look at the raw data from the replication attempts, three spreadsheets side by side, two of which disagreed with each other and all of which disagreed with the original in small ways. "This is what it looks like before it becomes a fact," she said. Tristan copied the numbers into his notebook, then took out his report and, in the margin beside the bold hypothesis, wrote a small asterisk and beneath it: one source, unreviewed, unreplicated, see also: everything.

On the bus home he composed two emails in his head, one to the committee and one to nobody, and sent neither yet. Rachael slept against the window and Marko was watching a video with the sound off. Tristan unfolded the report one more time, looked at the asterisk, and then held the page out over the aisle. "Read the margin," he said. "Tell me if it sounds like a retraction or an excuse."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
story:
Clara had claimed the carrel by the periodicals window because it was the one place in the library where nobody could stand behind her, and for two hours she had been failing to write the essay that was due on Friday. The prompt sat at the top of her notebook in Ms. Campbell-Brown's tidy hand: Which explanation of the Cold War's origins does the evidence better support? Below it, two open books, one on either side of her like witnesses who refused to look at each other.

The first was the textbook, all magisterial calm, which laid the blame on Soviet aggression and ideology. The second was the book she had found at her grandmother's house last weekend, in a cardboard box of her late grandfather's things, its spine cracked and its cover soft with handling. She had picked it up expecting a slog and had been startled by the argument instead. She read the title page again now, as if it might have changed overnight. William Appleman Williams, 1959, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. Her grandfather, a man who had flown transport planes in the sixties, had owned a book by an American who blamed his own country.

At the next carrel, Thalia was highlighting her own textbook with such vigor that the pages looked bruised. "You're staring at that thing again," Thalia said without looking up. "The old one."

"It's the revisionist one," Clara said. "That's what it's called. It started a whole school."

Thalia turned a page. "Weird thing for your grandpa to have."

That was the problem, or one of them. Clara had gone back to her grandmother's on Tuesday to ask about it, and her grandmother had gone quiet in a way Clara had never seen, wiping her hands on a dish towel that was already dry. "That was his college copy," she'd said finally. "He kept everything from those years." Then she had started talking about the rhubarb coming up early, and Clara had let her, and had not asked the question she actually wanted to ask, which was what a young man in the fifties had believed when he read a book like that, and whether he had stopped.

She made herself work. On the left page of her notebook she listed the orthodox case: the takeover of Eastern Europe, the blockade of Berlin, Stalin's secrecy. On the right she listed Williams's claim, which was stranger and harder: that American economic expansion helped cause the conflict, that the drive for open markets had its own logic, its own pressure. She had expected the revisionist argument to feel like an accusation. Instead it felt like a lens being slowly turned, and ordinary scenes coming into focus differently.

What she could not do was make the two columns talk to each other. The textbook treated Soviet behavior as the whole question. Williams treated American behavior as the question. When she tried to hold both in her head at once, she felt like she was prevaricating with herself, telling each side what it wanted to hear rather than committing to anything. Ms. Campbell-Brown had warned them about this in her dry way, saying that a lazy historian lets sources merge into mush, and that perspicacity meant seeing what each source left out, not just what it said. Clara had written the word down then; now she underlined it.

Anabel arrived at four with a bag of clementines and a talent for interrupting at exactly the wrong moment. She dropped into the third chair, saw Clara's face, and lowered her voice. "Bad?"

"I found something in my grandpa's boxes," Clara said. "A book that basically says the US helped cause the Cold War. William Appleman Williams, 1959. The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. It began the revisionist school." She heard herself reciting it like a defense. "And the textbook says it was the Soviets. And I don't know which one the evidence actually favors, or whether that's even the right question."

Anabel peeled a clementine in one long ribbon and offered half. "So what did your grandmother say?"

"She said the rhubarb came up early." Clara took her half and didn't eat it. "Which is why I came here instead of asking her again. There's something she's not telling me. Or something she's saving."

The light moved across the periodicals, and the library got quieter the way it does when the after-school crowd drains away. Clara went back to the primary source packet Ms. Campbell-Brown had assigned, the long telegram and the Truman Doctrine speech and a page from a State Department planning memo she had skimmed and dismissed. She read it again now, slowly, and found a sentence about access to world markets that could belong in either book. She copied it out and drew an arrow from each column toward it, and then sat with the arrow, because it didn't settle anything. Both stories could contain that sentence. The evidence didn't line up behind one of them; it kept splitting, and the more she read, the less the split looked like a flaw in her method and the more it looked like the actual shape of the thing.

Thalia leaned over, read the arrowed sentence upside down, and whistled softly. "You're going to hand in an essay that says 'both, sort of, and here's what I still can't tell'? Campbell-Brown will eat you."

"She might." Clara closed the notebook and slid the two books into her bag, Williams on top of the textbook, spine to spine. "Or she might not." She stood, and the late sun caught the window glass, and out past the parking lot she could see the bus that went to her grandmother's neighborhood pulling up to the stop, its door already folding open.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
story:
Anthony found the blood pressure cuff in his grandfather's bathroom cabinet, wedged behind the laxatives and a rusted tin of shaving powder, and he brought it home on the bus balanced on his knees like something that might go off. The presentation was tomorrow. Ms. Sinclair had assigned it in September, back when the semester felt infinite, and had spent October repeating that half of the class would fail if they explained the reading without explaining the life behind the reading. He had two days of notes on systolic and diastolic numbers and no idea, still, what any of it meant in a human arm.

He sat on the edge of the bathtub and worked the Velcro strap around his own bicep. The instructions were printed in four languages, and in each of them the diagrams showed a calm, middle-aged man, which Anthony was not. He pressed the button. The cuff gripped him with startling force, a machine's unembarrassed handshake, and then the numbers came up on the little screen and meant nothing to him at all. He copied them into his phone and copied them again an hour later, and they were not the same, and this frightened him more than either number would have alone.

At school, Quinten looked at the spreadsheet of readings over his shoulder and did not bother to lower his voice. "It's a fitness unit, not an actuarial table," he said. "Nobody wants your grandfather's home medical data for nine minutes." Lyvia, who sat near the window and rarely spoke during these exchanges, leaned across the aisle. "Actually I'd want that. My dad has one of those cuffs and nobody in my house knows how to read it. What does yours say?" Anthony admitted that he didn't know what it said, only what it was, and Quinten rolled his eyes and denigrated the whole project, the unit, and, by extension, Ms. Sinclair's taste in assignments, though he said it with a grin that took the sting out.

That afternoon Anthony went back to his grandfather's apartment, ostensibly to return the cuff. The old man was in his chair watching a game with the sound off, and he waved Anthony toward the bathroom without turning his head. "Take it off the sink," he said. "And check the cabinet, there's soup in there for you." There was, in fact, a can of chicken noodle on the shelf beside the laxatives, and while Anthony stood there holding it, waiting for the right moment to go back out, he turned it over and read the label. Sodium, per serving, and then the number of servings in the can. He stood in that small tiled room doing the arithmetic twice, because it didn't seem possible. One can was nearly half of what the World Health Organization recommended for an entire day. Less than two grams of sodium, he remembered from somewhere, and that was less than five grams of salt, and the can in his hand was a large fraction of it before you counted the salt shaker on the table, the bread, the cold cuts in the drawer.

He came out slowly, holding the can. "Grandpa, how many of these do you eat a week?" His grandfather considered the question the way he considered referees' calls, with a tolerant shrug. "Three, four. Your grandmother used to make it from scratch, but that's a production." Anthony sat down on the ottoman and did more arithmetic, silently, and did not like the total. Two different thoughts were pulling at him: one was Quinten's, that this was just a project, numbers you arranged and presented and then forgot; the other was heavier, and he couldn't yet give it a sentence.

He took the readings that evening, in the bathroom, with the door open and his grandfather's sleeve rolled up, because the old man's hearing was bad and Anthony wanted him to hear the explanation anyway. He wrapped the cuff, pressed the button, watched the dial climb and settle, and then kept his face very still, because the screen was telling him something he had not expected, something he did not want to say out loud in a tiled room at suppertime. He had seen his own numbers all week. These were not those numbers. He took it again, carefully, the way the instructions said, feet flat, arm at heart level, and the machine confirmed itself.

"Tell me," his grandfather said, watching his face rather than the screen. "I'm eighty-one, I don't need it softened."

Anthony exhaled. "It's high. Not a little high. And I read your soup cans, and you're over the daily limit almost every day before dinner. The WHO says under two grams of sodium, which is under five grams of salt, and one can of that soup is nearly half the day." He paused, deciding against a speech; he could feel a peroration building in his chest, all the material from his notes, and he swallowed it. "I don't know if that's why the number is what it is. I can't know that part. But you could eat less of it. And you could walk with me after school."

His grandfather looked at the muted television for a while. Outside, a car went past with its radio too loud. "You'd come here every day?" he asked. "In November?"

"I'd come," Anthony said. He deflated the cuff and folded it, and set it on the sink where it had lived for years, and his grandfather turned the television's sound back on.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The apartment smelled like burnt popcorn and salsa, which meant his mother had been cooking in a hurry again. Tyler claimed the good corner of the couch an hour before kickoff, partly because he wanted it and partly because Sawyer had texted ARE YOU SERIOUSLY HOSTING and someone had to defend the territory. By the time the game started there were nine people in the living room: his mother, his stepfather, Sawyer, Melinda, two neighbors from down the hall, and Tyler's little cousin, Desmond, who was eleven and had been dropped off with a bag of chips and instructions to be good.

Tyler wanted one thing from the afternoon, and it was smaller than anyone would have guessed. He wanted to explain something to Desmond. Not in a lecturing way, not the way his stepfather explained things, with that patient voice that made you feel like a sink being fixed. He wanted to actually show his cousin something true and watch it land, because the last time he'd tried, at Thanksgiving, it had gone badly. He'd told Desmond that the moon didn't make its own light, and Desmond had said, "Then how does it glow, genius," and Tyler had lost his temper, and the whole table had gone quiet in that awful way.

Midway through the first quarter, Desmond leaned forward off the ottoman and pointed at the screen. "Why do they paint the line yellow right before the play? How do the guys not slip on the paint?"

Tyler opened his mouth and then closed it, because this was exactly the moment, and he did not want to waste it. Sawyer was already grinning. "Dude, they repaint it every down? The grounds crew is fast," Sawyer said, laying it on thick, and Desmond nodded slowly, buying it, and something in Tyler's chest went tight. It would be a travesty, he thought, to let the kid walk around believing that. Some lies were funny for ten seconds and then they were just lies.

"It's not painted," Tyler said. He kept his voice level. "It's drawn on by a computer. The line you see on the TV, the players can't see it at all. It's not on the field."

Desmond squinted at him with the exact same face from Thanksgiving. "Then how does it stay on the grass when the guys run over it?"

"You're watching the broadcast," Tyler said. "The line is part of the broadcast. Like the score in the corner. It's a company that figured out how to do it, Sportvision. The first time anybody saw it was on ESPN, September 27, 1998." He'd found this out two years ago, down a rabbit hole that had started because he'd wondered the same thing Desmond was wondering, and had ended with him reading old articles on his phone at one in the morning, melancholic in a way he couldn't explain, thinking about how something could be everywhere and brand new at once.

Melinda, who had been half-watching from the armchair with a bowl she wasn't sharing, looked up. "Wait, seriously? I always thought there was some kind of projector."

"It looks so real, though," Desmond said.

"I know." Tyler took out his phone. "Watch this." He pulled up a clip from a game, an old one, grainy, no yellow line anywhere, just green field and players and the old graphics. Desmond watched it with his mouth slightly open. On the television, the current game broke for a timeout, and Tyler pointed between the two screens, the line-less past and the line-filled present. "Fifteen years before you were born, everybody watched like that. Then one game in '98, there's this line, and now it's weird to see a game without it."

"Can I see the Sportvision thing?" Desmond asked, and Tyler handed him the phone, and for a while the room went quiet except for the announcers and Desmond scrolling, and Tyler sat back and let it be. He knew, in some part of himself that was honest even when it was inconvenient, that he hadn't explained how the computer did it, because he didn't fully understand it, and he knew that Desmond might still half-believe in paint. Wanting to hand somebody the whole truth, clean and complete, might problematize the whole project of explaining things, since even the explainer was working from secondhand articles at one in the morning. But this was different from the moon. This time Desmond had asked. This time nobody's voice had gotten sharp.

Sawyer drained the last of his soda and said, "You just ruined grounds crews everywhere, Ty."

"Improved them," Tyler said. "Fewer painters, fewer slips."

Desmond looked up from the phone, eyes narrowed, working through something. "So the line is there and not there at the same time?"

"Basically," Tyler said, and Desmond nodded slowly, the way a person nods when a door has opened and they're deciding whether to walk through it. Then Desmond turned back to the screen as the teams lined up, third down and four, and pointed at the yellow stripe stretched across the grass that only they could see. "Okay, but if it's not real, how come everybody's acting like it is?"
